A few words to know

undelivered
Not reaching the intended person.
follow-up
A later action taken to check or resolve something.

Changed so individuals cannot be identified.

Someone who looks after historical records.
correspondence

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The dispatch register had given Emma a set of dates, but not the confirmation of receipt she needed. If a student had fourteen days from receiving a decision to request a review, a record of posting was only part of the story.

Fiona Bell sent her another document: a page from the trust's 2011 office manual headed “Returned correspondence”. It instructed staff to check an address when a letter came back undelivered, attempt further contact and record what action had been taken.

Emma phoned Fiona.

“Have you found any completed records of those follow-ups?”

“Not yet. And the manual doesn't tell us whether these instructions were always followed.”

“Would it cover letters that were lost without being returned?”

“Nothing on this page explains that.”

Emma wrote the limitations beside the document. A sensible procedure could exist without being used consistently. Equally, a missing record did not establish that staff had ignored a problem.

Sarah suggested asking for a count of returned decision notices, rather than individual names. Emma sent Fiona a narrow request along those lines, making clear that anonymised totals or a description of surviving records would be sufficient.

Meanwhile, a member of the newspaper archive contacted Emma. The private correspondence collection remained closed pending checks, but staff could search an old subject index. The index did not reproduce the letters, and its descriptions could be incomplete.

That afternoon the archivist identified a single entry from October 2011 labelled “Student Travel — decision not received”. No author was named in the material shared with Emma. Nor was the text of the letter available.

Sarah was excited. “We finally have a student saying a decision never arrived.”

“Perhaps,” Emma said, “but we have an index entry. We don't know whether the writer was a student, a parent or someone else. We don't even know exactly what the complaint said.”

“Could it be the September parent?”

“There's no basis for joining them yet.”

Emma recorded the exact wording and the archive reference. She also noted that an October letter could have concerned any stage of the scheme. Its title alone did not establish a missed deadline or an improperly denied appeal.

By evening Fiona had replied again. The manual did not describe reminders to applicants who failed to respond, and the records team had not yet confirmed any returns log. It was a gap worth examining, not grounds for an accusation.

Emma returned to the three headings she had used the previous day: Prepared, Sent, Received. Beneath them she added a fourth: Able to appeal.

The first two might be reconstructed from the ledger. The third required other evidence. And the fourth depended on more than delivery alone: a student had to understand the decision and the review procedure in time to act.

For the first time, the correspondence trail raised a question about access, not merely administration. Emma still needed the original October letter before she could judge what had gone wrong, if anything.
